title: Why God had the law written — then why leave any equal part unwritten?
source_text: XXXIV. Atque, ut adversarios hic magis constringamus, rogamus eos quare Deus tandem voluit legem suam scripto mandari, & reliquum Scripturae sacrae corpus confici. Certe negare non possunt, quin id factum voluerit Deus, tum ut succurreretur humanae infirmitati, tum ut occurreretur fraudibus impiorum: & quin fuerit Dei consilium, doctrinam sacram istis libris contentam, ab hominum oblivione, & corruptelis vindicare, & tutam illam reddere contra aliorum quidem negligentiam, aliorum vero fraudes & imposturas. Quandequidem autem res ita se habet, dicant adversarii cur toti doctrinae sacrae Deus ita consultum noluit; sed unam quidem partem scribi voluit, aliam vero non scriptam remanere. Etenim, an pars illa non scripta minus opportuna est fraudibus diabolicis, & oblivioni minus obnoxia, quam pars illa quae scripto mandata est? Et nonne testatur experientia in toto orbe, ubi defuit Scriptura, mansisse quidem nonnulla vestigia divinae doctrinae a Patribus traditae, sed illa fabulis miserandum in modum contaminata fuisse, ritusque sacrilegos & peregrinos introductos, & in horrendam, ut diximus, idololatriam detortos? Adde quod adversarii inter causas, quibus divinam providentiam uti volunt in traditionibus conservandis, numerant scripta Doctorum hominum, quibus consignatae sint. Si ergo opus fuit traditiones scribi quo facilius conservari possent, cur Deus id factum voluisset potius ab hominibus vulgaribus & errori obnoxiis, quam a Prophetis atque Apostolis, quibus caetera doctrinae salutaris capita scribenda mandavit? Et cur, si ea quae ex traditione peti volunt ejusdem momenti sunt cum iis quae sacra Scriptura continentur, haec tabulis authenticis consignari voluit, ista vero in hominum vulgarium scriptis relinquere?
pass_a_gloss: And so that we may constrain the adversaries more tightly here, we ask them why God at last willed His law to be committed to writing, and the remaining body of sacred Scripture to be composed. Certainly they cannot deny that God willed this to be done, both that human infirmity might be helped, and that the frauds of the ungodly might be met; and that it was God's counsel to vindicate the sacred doctrine contained in those books from men's oblivion and corruptions, and to render it safe against the negligence of some and the frauds and impostures of others. But since the matter stands thus, let the adversaries say why God did not will the same care for the whole of sacred doctrine; but willed one part indeed to be written, and another to remain unwritten. For is that unwritten part less open to diabolical frauds, and less liable to oblivion, than the part committed to writing? And does not experience testify throughout the whole world that where Scripture was lacking, some vestiges of divine doctrine handed down from the Fathers did remain, but that they were contaminated by fables in a pitiable way, and sacrilegious and foreign rites were introduced, and twisted into horrible idolatry, as we have said? Add that among the causes by which the adversaries claim divine providence uses to conserve traditions, they number the writings of learned men in which the traditions are consigned. If therefore it was necessary that traditions be written so that they might more easily be conserved, why would God have willed that done rather by common men liable to error than by the Prophets and Apostles, to whom He commanded the other heads of saving doctrine to be written? And why, if the things they want drawn from tradition are of the same moment as those contained in sacred Scripture, did He will these to be consigned to authentic tables, but those to be left in the writings of common men?
pass_b_english: Press harder: why did God finally will His law written, and the rest of sacred Scripture composed?

Rome cannot deny the twin aims — to help human weakness and to block the frauds of the ungodly — and that God's counsel was to rescue the doctrine in those books from oblivion and corruption, and keep it safe against negligence and imposture.
Then why not the same care for the whole of sacred doctrine? Why write one part and leave another equal part unwritten?
Is the unwritten part somehow less open to diabolical fraud and forgetfulness than the written part?
Worldwide experience says otherwise: where Scripture was missing, Father-handed vestiges remained, but ruined by fables, foreign sacrilegious rites, and idolatry.

Rome itself counts later doctors' writings among providence's means of keeping traditions. If traditions needed writing to survive, why leave that writing to fallible common authors instead of Prophets and Apostles — and why seal Scripture on authentic tables while parking equal-weight traditions in ordinary men's books?
